analysis.one_liner: Shuts down the Department of Education on the last day of 2026.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three Senate sponsors in March 2025, the bill has received no hearing, markup, or vote and sits in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would abolish the Department of Education on December 31, 2026. It says nothing about what would happen to the programs the department runs — Pell Grants, federal student loans, Title I money for low-income schools, special education funding, and federal enforcement of student civil rights. As written, those programs would lose their administrative home.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers would save whatever the department itself costs to run, though the bill does not say whether the programs it administers would end or move elsewhere. If federal student loans and grants end with the department, private student lenders and loan servicers gain a larger market. States would gain full control over education policy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private student lenders and states seeking control

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the federal department and its budget outright, on a fixed date, with no replacement structure.

The bill is a single sentence: 'The Department of Education shall terminate on December 31, 2026.' It contains no provisions for transferring Pell Grants, student loans, Title I, or special education funding to another agency.

analysis.who_pays: Students and families would risk losing Pell Grants and federal student loans, which about 7 million students use each year, or face them moving to a private market with fewer protections. Low-income school districts would risk losing Title I funding, and school districts everywhere would risk losing the federal share of special education costs. Students relying on federal oversight of loan servicing and campus civil rights enforcement would lose their advocate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Students, loan borrowers, and low-income schools

drawbacks.text: The bill terminates the department without any plan for the programs it administers, leaving Pell Grants, federal student loans, Title I school funding, and special education grants with no designated agency to run them.
Federal student aid and enforcement of borrowers' rights and campus civil rights would either disappear or move to private markets and state-level enforcement with fewer uniform protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings from closing the department's own operations are small next to the value of the aid it distributes, and the bill never says whether that aid survives. For the millions of families that depend on Pell Grants, federal loans, and special education funding, the risk outweighs the savings, and the bill's brevity is the core problem: it ends the machinery without answering what happens to the people who use it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and has sat there since with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on March 26, 2025, with Senators Mike Lee and Bernie Moreno as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody has won or lost on the merits — federal education aid continues as before, and the bill's only effect to date is to place the proposal on the record with three sponsors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; nothing has happened

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Department of Education.

for.name: 2 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Bernie Moreno of Ohio)

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 26, 2025, and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote is listed in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Republicans and no other senator has signed on, but with no hearing or vote in the record there is no way to see where the parties as a whole stand.

industries.industry: Private student lenders and loan servicers
industries.note: If the department ends and federal loans end with it, borrowers needing credit would turn to private lenders, which charge more and offer fewer protections. The bill does not spell this out, but ending the department leaves federal lending with no home.

industries.industry: Public school districts, especially low-income ones
industries.note: Districts receive Title I funds for low-income students and a federal share of special education costs administered by the department. Losing the department without a replacement puts that money in doubt.

The Department of Education is the main federal regulator of for-profit colleges, including loan servicing and accreditation oversight. Ending it removes that oversight; the bill provides nothing in its place.
Taxpayers would save the department's administrative costs, but the bill is silent on whether the aid programs it funds would also end or continue elsewhere, so the net fiscal effect is unknown.

analysis.trajectory: A one-sentence agency-termination bill with three sponsors and no committee action five months in is unlikely to move. Its author chairs the committee it was referred to, and still no hearing has been scheduled, which usually signals the bill is intended as a statement of position rather than a serious legislative push.
